newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA NANDO'S OFFER CLOSES, FIRM DEBUT SEEN FRI.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA NANDO'S OFFER CLOSES, FIRM DEBUT SEEN FRI.

text.p: A public share offer by South Africa's Nando's Chickenland, which is to be listed on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE) on Friday, closed at noon (1000 GMT) on Tuesday, sponsoring brokers Fleming Martin said.

Market watchers said the offer by the fast-food company, which is expected to score a flying debut with some 192.74 million shares in the JSE's beverages, hotel and leisure sector, is seen heavily over-subscribed.
"There seems to be enormous interest, but I think we'll have to wait (for Friday) and see," Bobby Favish, Nando's chief financial officer told Reuters.
A spokesman for Fleming Martin told Reuters that the results of the offer, in which 15 million Nando's shares of 100 cents each were offered to the public, will be made known on Thursday.
Another 10 million shares have been offered to business associates and employees in a preferential offer.

Nando's, which has shown heady growth in number of outlets and profits in the past 10 years and more recently moved aggressively offshore, has forecast earnings growth at 6.25 cents a share in the year to end-February 1998, compared with an historical figure of 5.15 the year before.
Favish said Nando's plans dividend cover of 2.5 times although not in the first year as it was not a full 12 months period.
"We anticipate a lot of growth locally, we are basically focused on our Nando's brand, but we have several other concepts we are working on," Favish said.
The group has opened two new full-service restaurants, Tasca, and plans to develop a food-court concept. It also brands a range of sauces and salad dressings to accompany its flame-grilled chicken.

"There's a lot of hype about it. The man-in-the-street knows a lot about it. It is seen to be a good marketer, the market thinks it is a high growth company," said an analyst who asked not to be identified.
Willi Jonker, executive director of portfolio management at Norwich Investments, said the relatively small public offer meant a bigger scramble for shares.
"They are not swamping the market with shares, so that more people want shares than are being offered. I think it's going to be a good listing," Jonker said.
But other analysts raised concerns about Nando's limited exposure to its overseas businesses, where good growth prospects were seen.
"The international rights to use the brand and trademark are held in a company to which the company in South Africa only has a profit participation and not ownership," said another analyst.
"That, I think is one of the things the market may not like, and we may see the share price coming off after the listing," she said.
